item.title: 🔵 Autonomy creep: how AI quietly gains more authority than CIOs intend
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Few CIOs are likely to suddenly decide to give an AI agent broad authority over corporate systems. The more likely path to autonomy is far less dramatic. An agent starts with a narrow task. It proves useful, so another system is connected. It then needs more data, so another permission is added. Then human approval becomes a bottleneck, so the organization removes it, and exceptions that once went to people start being handled automatically.

Each decision may be sensible in isolation. Taken together, however, they can leave an agent with considerably more authority than anyone originally envisioned.

item.description:

For years, disaster recovery was built around a relatively simple question: How quickly can we get the business back online?

That question still matters. But for today’s CIO, it is no longer enough.

Enterprise technology environments have become too dynamic to define recovery simply as restoring applications, reconnecting infrastructure and resuming operations. Applications span on-premises infrastructure, cloud environments and SaaS platforms. Identities and permissions are constantly changing. Employees introduce new tools and automation into workflows, sometimes without IT knowing about them. AI is accelerating that pace of change even further.

As a CIO, I see this complexity firsthand. My organization is navigating its own transformation while modernizing the technology that supports the business. item.title: 🔵 The inference path is where AI value is won or lost
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

As organizations incorporate AI into their environments, they’re hyper-focused on the AI model. Many executives I talk to spend a lot of time considering what model they should purchase from which vendor. They’re also concerned about which use case they should implement first.

Yet the reality is that AI models are swappable components. The vast majority of organizations are using multiple AI models, switching them out for their specific needs based on cost, accuracy, and security. It’s the right thing to do; organizations with architectures that make it difficult to swap out AI models are making the wrong bet.

What can’t be swapped out is your inference path—or everything that happens between a user’s intent and the model’s output. This includes the retrieval layer that decides what context the model sees. It includes the routing logic that chooses what model handles which request. It includes the identity that travels with the call. IT leaders seeking promising AI use cases may be overlooking a potential goldmine: deploying the technology to assist with major IT modernization and digital transformation initiatives.

Leading CIOs at a handful of large enterprises have leveraged generative AI and related tools to rewrite code, redesign workflows, and migrate databases during major digital transformation efforts, a practice that isn’t as widespread as its potential suggests.

“The potential is actually, I don’t want to say ‘limitless,’ but it is,” says Vijay Thangella, head of AI and machine learning at contact center technology provider Avaya. “There’s a very high potential.”

Avaya, using AI tools built from frontier models, claims it can help customers cut contact-center modernization timelines drastically. Revamping legacy contact centers typically requires IT teams to spend months deciphering and manually rebuilding years of workflows, routing logic, integrations, and business rules. AI-assisted modernization can cut the time to a few days, Thangella says.

item.title: 🔵 OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
item.description:

Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices.

A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems.

Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL).
